one_liner: Book sample: one OpenMP 'parallel for' min-reduction pragma on an O(n^2) closest-pair loop, about 4x over one thread.
what_it_does: A chapter-4 companion sample from a Packt C++ book: two functions with the same signature, float f(std::span<const Point2D>), that return the smallest Euclidean distance between any two points (the closest-pair distance) by checking every pair. The OpenMP version is the sequential double loop plus one '#pragma omp parallel for reduction(min:min_distance)' line on the outer loop; it returns only the distance, not which pair. A Google Benchmark driver times both on 65,536 random float points in [-1,1]^2.
how_it_is_fast: Plain fork-join thread parallelism: OpenMP splits the outer loop's rows across a team of threads (one per logical CPU by default), each thread keeps a private minimum, and the min reduction combines them at the end. The per-pair work is unchanged (one std::hypot call per pair) and the algorithm stays O(n^2). The rows are triangular (row i does n-i-1 pairs) and there is no schedule clause, so under the usual static schedule the first of 8 threads gets about 23% of all pairs, which caps the speedup near 4.3x (derived from the code); the reported 4.1x sits right at that cap.
when_to_use: As a minimal template for parallelising an embarrassingly parallel outer loop that ends in a scalar min, max or sum reduction, in code that already builds with OpenMP.

Brute-force all-pairs kernels on a few thousand to tens of thousands of points where writing a spatial index is not worth it; the min reduction is exact and order-independent, so the result is identical to the sequential loop.
Teaching or measuring OpenMP scaling and load imbalance on a multi-core desktop, where the gap between 4.1x and 8x is itself the lesson.
when_not_to_use: Closest-pair search on large point sets: a divide-and-conquer or sweep-line closest-pair algorithm, or a uniform grid or k-d tree, is O(n log n), about a million steps at n = 65,536 against 2.1 billion pair checks here, which no thread count makes up for (derived).
When you need the pair itself (the two indices); the functions return only the minimum distance.

Toolchains without an OpenMP runtime: find_package(OpenMP REQUIRED) fails where none is installed (AppleClang does not ship one by default), and MSVC needs the experimental runtime that the CMake file selects for reduction(min).
Code that already runs inside its own thread pool or several application threads: each call opens its own OpenMP team, so concurrent callers oversubscribe the cores.
Small inputs: only 65,536 points are benchmarked, so the size below which thread start-up and the final barrier outweigh the gain is not documented.

integration.form: source-drop (two functions in Chapter-04/nearest_neighbor.cpp plus a short header; the speedup is a single pragma)
integration.dependencies: an OpenMP runtime (libgomp, LLVM libomp or MSVC's); the benchmark needs Google Benchmark, and the shared Chapter-04 CMake project also requires GTest and Threads at configure time (BLAS optional)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (std::span; the benchmark's emplace_back on the aggregate Point2D needs parenthesised aggregate initialisation, GCC 10+ or Clang 16+), OpenMP 3.1+ for reduction(min), CMake 3.30+ as the CMakeLists requires
integration.platforms: any OS and CPU with an OpenMP-capable C++20 compiler; no ISA-specific code
integration.thread_safety: Reentrant (reads a const span and returns a value), but every call starts an OpenMP parallel region; concurrent calls from several threads oversubscribe the cores, and calls nested inside another parallel region usually run with one thread.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same signature and the same result as nearest_neighbor_distance_seq, but the translation unit must be compiled with the OpenMP flag (-fopenmp, /openmp) and linked against the runtime; without it the pragma is ignored and the code runs sequentially.

gotchas: No schedule clause on a triangular loop: with the default static schedule thread 0 gets rows 0-8191, about 503 million of the 2.15 billion pairs, so 8 threads cannot exceed about 4.3x; schedule(dynamic, chunk), schedule(guided) or pairing row i with row n-1-i should balance the work (derived from the code, not measured).

Each pair calls std::hypot, which guards against overflow and is slower than sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy); comparing squared distances and taking one sqrt at the end lightens the inner loop for both versions and makes it a candidate for auto-vectorisation, so SIMD and threads could compound (derived, not measured).

The benchmark does not call UseRealTime(); Google Benchmark's default CPU timer measures only the main thread, so read the wall-clock Time column for the OpenMP row. At 1-5 s per call the default 0.5 s minimum time is met after one iteration, so each figure is probably a single call unless --benchmark_repetitions was passed (derived from the Google Benchmark user guide).

Chapter-04/CMakeLists.txt sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so a plain configure builds without optimisation; configure Release to compare. Open PR #14 (December 2025, unmerged) fixes build errors in the same chapter's gemm files (a missing matrix.h include, asserts naming undeclared a, b, c), so build the bench_nearest_neighbor target on its own if the full project fails.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the SIMD siblings (xsimd, Vc, NumKong) add threads; use this pattern when the kernel is already acceptable per element and idle cores are the cheapest win, and reach for NumKong or xsimd to speed up the per-pair arithmetic instead (the two combine; NumKong's distance kernels target long vectors rather than 2-D points).
verified_claims_summary: The repository holds code only; the book's run, relayed by the seed lead, gives 4,797 ms for the sequential all-pairs loop and 1,161 ms with OpenMP on 8 threads over 65,536 random float points (about 4.1x), timed with Google Benchmark against the same author's single-threaded loop. Compiler, flags, OpenMP runtime and CPU model are not stated, and the repository's CMake sets no optimisation level.
status_note: Packt book companion repository, MIT-licensed, 20 stars and 8 forks; the last commit (2026-01-22) changed only the README and the code last changed in November 2025, with one open issue (#15, about the chapter-4 clamp loop) and one unmerged build-fix PR (#14); the technique is a single pragma, so there is nothing to vendor.
